Write a function that allows the user to query this API.

querynews <- function(subject, time, key){
  
  getresult <- GET(paste0("https://newsapi.org/v2/everything?q=", 
                          gsub(" ", "%20", subject), 
                          "&from=", 
                          time, 
                          "&language=en&pageSize=50&apiKey=", 
                          key))
  
  parsedresult <- fromJSON(rawToChar(getresult$content))
  return(as_tibble(parsedresult$articles))

What is meant by long format data and wide format data? Which do we generally prefer for statistical analysis?

What is meant by long format data and wide format data?

Long format is a data table organization where each row is one observation and each column is a variable. Repeated measures are stored in additional rows. This is the ideal format when working with structured data for statistical analysis.
Wide format is where there can be multiple observations per row. Repeated measures are stored in additional columns instead of additional rows. Sometimes this makes the data easier to read in a table format.

Which do we generally prefer for statistical analysis? We generally prefer the long format to do analyses on. This enables us to do analysis on the variables and include each observation separately, not necessarily each individual though as some rows may be repeated measures on the same individual.

Task 1: Conceptual Questions

If your working directory is myfolder/homework/, what relative path would you specify to get the file located at myfolder/MyData.csv?
The relative path would be "../MyData.csv". The ../ moves from the working directory myfolder/homework/ up one level to the directory myfolder/.
What are the major benefits of using R projects?

Allows for the creation of a file hierarchy when working on one project that contains multiple files
Associated with a directory, which becomes the working directory for the project
Working directory can be used for coding using relative paths
When you render a .qmd file, the working directory for that rendering corresponds to the folder in which the .qmd file is located
Connects to Git and Github to allow for version control and collaboration, which can be managed directly in RStudio
Functions as a storage space for all information associated with a given project

What is Git and what is GitHub?
Git is version control software, which is useful for tracking changes to files and collaborating with others. GitHub is an online hosting service for Git-based projects, allowing your repository to be stored on the web and accessed remotely.
What are the two main differences between a tibble and a data.frame?
A tibble is a type of data.frame that is specific to the tidyverse package. The two main differences are:

The default print() method for a tibble has fancier printing: it shows the number of observations and columns and displays only the first few rows/columns.
tibbles do not coerce down to a vector when you subset to only one column using [.

Task 1: Conceptual Questions

To do this, you need to add “../”, so you would need read_csv("../MyData.csv"). ../ will take you one step “back” in your working directory, and then you can navigate from there.
R projects function as a storage space for all information associated with a given… project. They have a separate workspace, working directory, and source documents, making it simpler and easier to keep all relevant files in one place.
Git is a version control software that allows multiple people to remotely work on the same project simultaneously. GitHub is the online interface for this software, and it doubles as a public distribution system for those projects.
Tibbles and data frames are very similar, but the main differences are that

Tibbles do less guessing when used (i.e. no partial matching), so errors come up earlier

getIQR <- function(x){

Task 1: Conceptual Questions

If your working directory is myfolder/homework/, what relative path would you specify to get the file located at myfolder/MyData.csv?
The relative path would be "../MyData.csv". The ../ moves from the working directory myfolder/homework/ up one level to the directory myfolder/.
What are the major benefits of using R projects?
An R project is associated with a particular file folder, which becomes the working directory for the project. This works nicely with coding using relative paths. Also, when you render a .qmd file, the working directory for that rendering corresponds to the folder in which the .qmd file is located.
What is Git and what is GitHub?
Git is version control software, which is useful for tracking changes to files and collaborating with others. GitHub is an online hosting service for Git-based projects, allowing your repository to be accessed and stored on the web.
What are the two main differences between a tibble and a data.frame?

The default print() method for a tibble has fancier printing: it shows the number of observations and columns and displays only the first few rows/columns.
tibbles do not coerce down to a vector when you subset to only one column using [.

If your working directory is myfolder/homework/, what relative path would you specify to get the file located at myfolder/MyData.csv?


“../MyData.csv”


What are the major benefits of using R projects?


Allows for the creation of a file hierarchy when working on one project that contains multiple files
It’s association with a directory allows for ease in sharing/ collaborating
R projects can be connected with Git and GitHub to allow for version control and collaboration


What is Git and what is GitHub?


Git: a software that allows for version tracking of different projects.
GitHub: an online hosting service for Git projects that allows for storage and sharing of these projects.


What are the two main differences between a tibble and a data.frame?


A tibble is a type of data frame that is specific to the tidy verse package. A data frame cannot exist in the tidyverse if it’s not a tibble.
When a tibble is printed, we get information about the number of observations and see an output of the first few columns. When a data frame is printed, the output is generally the entire data frame regardless of the number of observations.
